clue.text: Getting away from van, going over a river is a bonus

indicators.note: one word going over another sits around it, so the bonus word wraps the pair

parts.note: a bonus is a reward

explanation.surface: A delivery driver earns extra pay for taking the van across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' is short for vanguard, the front, so moving away from it is heading backwards; it is not a vehicle here. 'going over' wraps REWARD around A and R.
explanation.definitionFit: The van is the leading part of an army, so moving away from the front means moving towards the back.

clue.text: Are now negotiating part for celebrity

indicators.note: part says only a portion of the phrase before it is used, a run of letters inside those words

explanation.surface: An agent is now negotiating a film role for a star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'negotiating' looks like an anagram signal for ARE NOW, but the letters fall one short; 'part' marks a run inside 'aRE NOW Negotiating'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fame or wide acclaim is the sense of celebrity meant here, not a famous person.

clue.text: Given job, copied about objective

indicators.note: about means around, so the copying word surrounds the aim

parts.note: aped means copied or imitated
the point is the objective or purpose

explanation.surface: Someone got a job by plagiarising their way to the goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given job' is the definition as a past participle, someone given a post; 'objective' is a noun, the aim, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Being named to a post means having been assigned to a role.

clue.text: Dancing girl going by air from Australia

parts.note: waltzing is one kind of dancing
Matilda is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl dances her way onto a flight out of Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' means a tune, not flight: the definition is a song from Australia, its unofficial anthem.
explanation.definitionFit: This famous bush ballad is a tune, an air, that comes from Australia.

clue.text: Jaunty, like our airmen?

definitions.meaning: rakish or carefree in a slightly disreputable way
read as RAF-ish, resembling members of the Royal Air Force

explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force; the suffix -ish means 'like', so the word splits as RAF-FISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Rakish, dashing flair is the sense, and split up it reads as resembling the Royal Air Force.

clue.text: In old inns he had stable employment

definitions.text: In old inns he had stable employment

parts.words: In old inns he had stable employment
parts.note: read literally, a man at a coaching inn whose job was looking after horses in the stables

explanation.definitionFit: The inn's groom who tended travellers' horses in the stable was given this title.

clue.text: Widely held view of Plato's Academy, say

definitions.meaning: a shared outlook or body of opinion
an institution of philosophical teaching, literally a place of learning devoted to ideas

explanation.definitionFit: A shared set of opinions, and literally a teaching establishment for ideas such as the Athenian philosopher's.

clue.text: No end of porridge for him?

definitions.text: No end of porridge for him?

parts.words: No end of porridge for him?
parts.note: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence, and for him it never ends

explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is British slang for time served in prison, so endless porridge means a sentence for the rest of one's life.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner serving a life sentence faces jail time with no end.

clue.text: Her deli's production found tasty

indicators.note: a production makes something new, so the letters are worked into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A customer enjoyed the food that a woman's delicatessen produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'production' rearranges the eight letters of HER DELIS, the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Enjoying food with great pleasure is to savour it.

clue.text: Fail to get American wife

parts.note: to miss is to fail to get
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A man fails to find an American bride.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal word for a man's spouse.

clue.text: Mountainous place where plane crashed

indicators.note: a plane that has crashed is wrecked, so its letters are scrambled into a new order

explanation.surface: A mountain country is named as the scene of an air crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashed' turns PLANE into a new five-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan kingdom holding Everest is a famously mountainous country.

clue.text: Legitimately entitled to follow fellow? Terrible!

indicators.note: the entitled word is told to come after the fellow, so it is placed second

parts.note: rightful means legitimately entitled

explanation.surface: Someone is outraged that a lawful heir must take second place to some chap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' puts RIGHTFUL after F.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean dreadful or very bad, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Successful young men whistling to children

parts.note: a whizz is a whistling or buzzing sound of something rushing past
kids are children

explanation.surface: Young high-flyers whistle at some children.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigies who achieve early success are called by this informal phrase.

clue.text: Men feared dying eventually in layers to be mined

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another, here the letter inside the mined material

parts.note: ores are mineral deposits dug from the ground

indicators.note: eventually points to the end of the word dying, its final letter

explanation.surface: Miners fear they will eventually die in the seams they dig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eventually' takes G, the last letter of 'dying', and 'in' puts it inside ORES.
explanation.definitionFit: Monsters of fairy tales are man-eating giants that people dread.

clue.text: This from first of spoiled fish?

definitions.text: This from first of spoiled fish?

indicators.note: first of picks out only the opening letter of the word spoiled

parts.note: a tench is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A rotten fish gives off a foul smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of' takes S from 'spoiled' and TENCH follows. Read as a whole, the clue says what a spoiled fish gives off.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotting fish gives off a strong foul smell, which the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Retention of herb covering hill

indicators.note: the herb covers the hill, so it goes around it

parts.note: sage is a culinary herb
a tor is a rocky hill, common in Dartmoor place names

explanation.surface: A herb grows over the top of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop of the kind found on Dartmoor in south-west England; 'Retention' is the definition, with 'of' only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping things put away for later use is the act of keeping or holding them.

clue.text: A stream conceals rabid old insectivore

indicators.note: one word concealing another holds it inside

parts.note: a rill is a small stream
rabid means mad

explanation.surface: A rabid animal hides out in a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabid old insectivore' reads as one noun phrase, but 'rabid' gives a word for mad and 'old' its own abbreviation, leaving 'insectivore' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This armoured American mammal feeds mainly on ants and other insects.

clue.text: Gallon sunk in royal house -this painful result?

indicators.note: something sunk in sits inside the other word

parts.note: Hanover is the royal house of the Georges who ruled Britain

explanation.surface: Drinking a gallon in a palace leads to suffering the next morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sunk in' puts G inside HANOVER, the German dynasty that ruled Britain from 1714 to 1901. A gallon 'sunk' also suggests heavy drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: The headache and nausea after heavy drinking are the unpleasant aftermath.

clue.text: Stomach shockingly bad portent

indicators.note: shockingly suggests something done badly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: an omen is a portent

explanation.surface: A gut feeling is taken as a very bad sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shockingly' rearranges BAD into ABD, followed by OMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The belly, holding the digestive organs, is the body region below the chest.

clue.text: Observing lack of sound from little bell?

parts.note: no means none, a lack of
ting is the light ringing sound of a small bell

explanation.surface: Someone watching notices a little bell has gone silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking notice of something is watching or remarking on it.

clue.text: Trouble getting air into narrow passages

definitions.text: Trouble getting air into narrow passages

parts.words: Trouble getting air into narrow passages
parts.note: describes a medical condition in which narrowed airways make breathing hard

explanation.definitionFit: This chronic illness constricts the bronchial tubes, causing wheezing and shortness of breath.

clue.text: Everything he'll say is simple

parts.note: all means everything

indicators.note: say means the word is spoken, so its sound counts rather than its spelling

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like HEAL

explanation.surface: Everything he says is easy to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: A simple is an old word for a medicinal herb; the answer is a plant, valerian or selfheal, used to heal all ills.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple is a medicinal herb, and this herb's name says it cures every ailment.

clue.text: Economist is cheerful

explanation.walkthrough: John Bright (1811-89) was a British radical who campaigned with Richard Cobden against the Corn Laws for free trade.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian free-trader shares his surname with the word for sunny and happy.

clue.text: No credit for this spirited author

definitions.text: No credit for this spirited author

parts.words: No credit for this spirited author
parts.note: a hired writer whose work appears under someone else's name gets no credit; spirited hints at a phantom

explanation.definitionFit: A hired writer working unseen is named after a phantom, and a phantom is a spirit.

clue.text: Ear, say, some musicians use to play

definitions.meaning: the ear is an example of a body part

explanation.definitionFit: A body part such as the ear, and the pipe instrument heard in churches.

clue.text: Tricky task to supply giraffes?

definitions.meaning: a demand that is hard to meet
an order for something lofty, as supplying giraffes would be

explanation.definitionFit: A daunting request is a big demand, and giraffes would make a lofty one to fill.

clue.text: He patrols street to deflect evil giant

indicators.note: deflecting knocks something off course, so the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: A street patrol tries to turn aside a wicked giant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to deflect' rearranges EVIL GIANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-appointed citizen enforcer keeps watch over his neighbourhood.

clue.text: With pistol shortly taking convict to camp

indicators.note: shortly says the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a pistol is a gun
a lag is slang for a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: An armed guard escorts a prisoner to a labour camp.
explanation.walkthrough: A lag is British slang for a convict, as in 'old lag'; 'With' and 'taking' only join the pieces, and 'to' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet forced-labour system ran prison camps under this name.

clue.text: Disheartened escapee found in part of airport

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle letter of the word goes

parts.note: a runaway is someone who has escaped

explanation.surface: A fugitive, losing heart, is found on the airfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disheartened' removes the central A from RUNAWAY.
explanation.definitionFit: The strip where planes take off and land is a section of the airfield.

clue.text: Policeman has rooms to pay for

parts.note: a flat is a set of rooms
to foot the bill is to pay for it

explanation.surface: An officer has a place to live that he must pay for.
explanation.walkthrough: FLATFOOT is old American slang for a patrolling police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated slang word for a beat cop, from the walking officer's tired feet.
